output.methodChoice: Kepner-Tregoe IS/IS-NOT specification (early action vs regular decision, tier), then competing-hypotheses comparison, with a source stake check.
output.brief: The evidence points mainly at the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office. Yield fell about 7.4 points in early action (legacy system, on-time decisions) and about 7.5 points in regular decision (late). The portal delay therefore doesn't explain the drop. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's went from $14,000 to $9,000 and yield from 45.2% to 31.9%. Merit went from $9,000 to $5,000 and yield from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards, unchanged, held at about 36%, and the no-award group held at about 37%. Applications and admit quality rose, so a weaker applicant pool and general demand softening don't fit. The 2021 elasticity estimate used to assure the board was evidently too optimistic. The slow regular-decision turnaround is real and worth fixing, but it didn't cause the yield fall, and I can't separate the reader cuts from the portal's scoring module. Whether the portal lost documents is unverified. Replacing the director would punish the wrong party. Next: take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the net-revenue trade-off modelled. Also set a turnaround target for regular decision. Hold the vendor rebuild until the document-loss claim is checked. Confidence is fairly high. The main gap is that the tier data doesn't split early action from regular decision.
